title: Operations agents — Oribos
description: Put agents on the operational busywork: your MCP tools, a cron, signal, or webhook to start, and a human on the risky steps. Runs suspend to a snapshot, not a resident worker.
positioning: Agents that handle the busywork around your team — with a human on the risky steps.

sections.heading: The work is repetitive. The mistakes are not.
sections.body:
The team already runs the systems: the ticketing queue, the billing ledger, the internal admin API. Much of the work around them is repetitive — triage this, reconcile that, draft the status note — but the work is not cheap to get wrong. The usual answers are a resident worker you now operate, or a workflow product that owns the logic somewhere you cannot inspect.

Oribos takes a third path. A cron expression, a signal, or a webhook starts a run in the process you already deploy. The agent calls the MCP tools your team exposes, and when a step crosses the line the run suspends with a JSON snapshot and waits for a person. Nothing executes while it waits, and the run's state is a JSON snapshot in a store you choose.

sections.heading: Three ways teams put an agent on operations
sections.intro: Each card is a path through the systems your team already runs. The packages are the only additions.

cards.name: Use the MCP tools you already run
cards.body: Tools from an existing MCP server become ordinary Oribos tools through `@oribos/mcp-client`, over HTTP or stdio. The bridged container is the same tool record an agent's `tools:` takes, so calls still go to the systems your team governs. There is no new tool registry and no second integration path.

cards.name: Put a human on the risky step
cards.body: A tool named on the durable wrapper's approval list does not execute: the run writes a snapshot, settles `'suspended'`, and returns control to your application. `resume(runId, { approved })` continues the same run from another process — approved executes the held call, rejected answers it with a rejection the model replans from. The ledger moves only after the decision.

cards.name: Wake on a schedule or a signal
cards.body: `@oribos/croner` turns one cron expression into the `next` fragment `schedules.save()` takes, and `tick` fires what is due when your platform's cron hits an endpoint. A signal wakes a run the same way, and `@oribos/background-tasks` carries app-owned work with at-least-once delivery. The process is yours; there is no Oribos worker to keep alive.

sections.heading: From a trigger to a snapshot
sections.body: The run exists while it executes. Between a trigger and a decision, the snapshot is the state.

flow.label: Cron, signal, or webhook
flow.detail: A platform cron, a signal, or an HTTP webhook calls your endpoint. `tick()` fires what is due; nothing polls in the background.

flow.label: Agent
flow.detail: An agent on `@oribos/core/agent` runs the loop in your process, with the tools you hand it.

flow.label: MCP tools
flow.detail: `@oribos/mcp-client` bridges existing MCP servers into ordinary tools; calls still hit the APIs your team governs.

flow.label: Approval gate
flow.detail: A held call does not execute: the run settles `'suspended'` with an `AgentRunSnapshotStore` snapshot.

flow.label: Snapshot store
flow.detail: The snapshot is a JSON port. `@oribos/sqlite` persists it; `resume(runId, { approved })` re-enters from another process.

tools.label: Where the human sits
tools.detail: Approval is a decision on the run, not an inbox. The person approves or rejects in the workflow or console your team already uses; the snapshot is the only state that crosses.

gate.label: Delivery semantics
gate.detail: `@oribos/background-tasks` is at-least-once and leaves idempotency to the application. `@oribos/distributed-signals` is at-most-once: a wake is not a durable queue.

sections.caption: Reference architecture, not a deployment diagram. Oribos runs no worker; the trigger endpoint and the snapshot store are yours.

sections.heading: Packages on this path
sections.intro: These published 0.9.0 packages cover the path above and its immediate edges. Install only the ones you use.

packages.name: @oribos/core
packages.purpose: Agents, tools, schedules, signals, the durable-agent approval gate, and storage ports.

packages.name: @oribos/mcp-client
packages.purpose: Remote MCP server tools as ordinary Oribos tools, over HTTP or stdio.

packages.name: @oribos/background-tasks
packages.purpose: App-owned background tasks with a lease, heartbeat, and settle; at-least-once.

packages.name: @oribos/distributed-signals
packages.purpose: Cross-instance signal routing with lease-arbitrated idle wake; at-most-once.

packages.name: @oribos/sqlite
packages.purpose: SQLite adapters for the memory, workflow snapshot, agent-run snapshot, and schedule ports.

sections.note: Every package here is published at 0.9.0. The core has zero runtime dependencies; capability packages carry only their own.

sections.heading: What Oribos is not
sections.intro: A solution page is also a boundary. These are deliberate.

items.title: Not an always-on worker
items.body: There is no resident process to keep alive. A platform cron, a signal, or a webhook starts work; between decisions the run is state in a snapshot store, not a loop in memory.

items.title: Not a workflow SaaS
items.body: The workflow, the triggers, and the records stay in your application. Oribos is a library you deploy, not a control plane you log in to.

items.title: Not a replacement for your operations tooling
items.body: The ticketing system, the ledger, and the admin API remain authoritative. Tools call them; Oribos does not copy their state or open a second path to it.

sections.heading: Runnable evidence
sections.intro: Each example is a program that asserts its own payoff. Run one before you trust this page.

items.name: mcp-tools
items.proves: Serves one tool container over MCP, bridges it back as a tool record over HTTP and stdio, and asserts the snapshot, both projections, the negative path, and refresh.

items.name: durable-approval
items.proves: Holds a refund at the approval gate, writes the loop snapshot, and resumes with approval or rejection. The ledger moves only after the decision.

items.name: cron-schedule
items.proves: Turns one expression into the `next` fragment `schedules.save()` takes, fires on `tick`, and asserts an early tick is a no-op and the record advances one day.

sections.heading: One expression, one saved schedule

items.q: Does this need a worker running all the time?
items.a: No. A platform cron, a signal, or a webhook calls an endpoint, and `tick()` fires what is due. A suspended run is a JSON snapshot in a store you choose; nothing runs while it waits.

items.q: What happens when the process dies mid-run?
items.a: With a persistent snapshot store, a suspended run resumes from its snapshot with `resume(runId, { approved })`; the default in-memory store does not survive a restart. `@oribos/background-tasks` is at-least-once and leaves idempotency to your application; `@oribos/distributed-signals` is at-most-once.

items.q: Do I have to move my operations tools into Oribos?
items.a: No. Existing MCP servers are bridged as-is, and plain HTTP tools work too. The ticketing system, ledger, and admin API stay authoritative.
